title: Excavating subsurface habitats in compacted regolith
bottleneck: Burying habitats under meters of regolith is the best radiation and micrometeorite shielding available — but lunar regolith below the fluffy surface is compacted and laced with rocks, and shadowed regions are frozen concrete-hard at -230 C. Excavation equipment must be lightweight for launch, autonomous, and able to operate in abrasive dust that destroys seals and bearings; terrestrial mining machines are far too heavy. No one has dug a habitat-scale cavity on another world.
why_it_blocks: Without subsurface construction, shielding mass must be launched from Earth at enormous cost; the buried-habitat concept is what makes long-term surface stays affordable.
current_state: NASA and ESA study excavation rovers; autonomous machines using percussive drills to break concrete-hard regolith are in lab testing. No off-world excavation beyond shallow scoops has been done.
